rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may use the Windows command shell (cmd.exe) to execute commands, launch processes, manipulate files, or perform discovery on a compromised host.
rules.how_it_works: An adversary can invoke the Windows command interpreter (cmd.exe) with execution parameters (such as /c or /k) or through batch files (.bat/.cmd) to run system utilities and secondary payloads indirectly through the operating system.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified technical evidence associated with Windows command shell execution.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may use the Windows command interpreter to execute commands or launch additional processes
rules.explanation: Command interpreter string 'cmd.exe' supports a possible command shell execution capability.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may use PowerShell commands and scripts to execute malicious code, interact with the operating system, and manipulate system objects.
rules.how_it_works: PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting language built on the .NET framework that adversaries leverage to execute code dynamically, bypass execution restrictions, and interact directly with Windows internals.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS observed technical evidence referencing PowerShell execution facilities or runtime scripts.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may invoke PowerShell to execute commands, download payloads, or manipulate system configuration
rules.explanation: References to powershell.exe support a possible PowerShell execution capability.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding entries to registry Run keys or placing shortcuts in the Windows startup folder to execute payloads upon system boot or user logon.
rules.how_it_works: Windows automatically executes programs referenced in specific registry keys (such as HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or HKLM\...\Run) when a user logs in or the operating system boots.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified registry path strings referencing autostart or Run locations.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may attempt to maintain persistence by configuring autostart registry keys
rules.explanation: Registry-path strings referencing Run or CurrentVersion locations support a possible persistence hypothesis.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable, payload, or string difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise packing file contents.
rules.how_it_works: Packers compress or encrypt the main executable payload and attach a stub that unpacks code directly into memory at runtime, concealing malicious logic and imports from static detection tools.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified high entropy sections or structural packing indicators within the binary.
rules.hypothesis: the binary structure exhibits entropy and packing indicators consistent with code obfuscation or compression
rules.explanation: Structural packing and entropy indicators support a possible obfuscation/evasion hypothesis.

rules.label: INFERRED
rules.description: Adversaries may inject code into running processes to evade process-based defenses, elevate privileges, or hide malicious execution under legitimate host processes.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries allocate memory in a target process using VirtualAllocEx, write shellcode or DLL paths with WriteProcessMemory, and execute the injected payload via CreateRemoteThread or asynchronous procedure calls (APCs).
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS detected function-level executable memory operations correlated with process manipulation APIs.
rules.hypothesis: the sample contains function logic and imported APIs that may facilitate remote process memory allocation or code injection
rules.explanation: Function-level executable memory allocation APIs support an inferred process manipulation or injection capability.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols (HTTP, HTTPS) to blend command and control traffic with legitimate web communications.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries establish outbound HTTP/HTTPS sessions to remote command-and-control servers using standard web ports (80, 443) to retrieve instructions and transmit collected data.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified network communication APIs combined with extracted URL, domain, or IP strings.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may initiate outbound application-layer HTTP/HTTPS network connections for command and control or telemetry communication
rules.explanation: Networking API capabilities combined with network indicators support possible command-and-control relevance.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols to blend command and control traffic with normal network operations.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries establish socket connections or transmit DNS queries to resolve remote domains and coordinate actions with command infrastructure.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS observed dynamic network connection telemetry or DNS queries during sandbox execution.
rules.hypothesis: runtime network telemetry indicates outbound socket or protocol communication consistent with network coordination
rules.explanation: Observed dynamic network connections support possible application-layer network coordination.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may achieve persistence by modifying startup registry keys to execute payloads when the system or user logs in.
rules.how_it_works: Programs writing values into Run/RunOnce registry locations ensure recurring execution on user session initialization.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS observed runtime registry modifications targeting autostart Run locations.
rules.hypothesis: observed runtime registry modifications indicate an attempt to establish autostart persistence
rules.explanation: Runtime registry modification in autostart locations supports possible persistence.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may search for and extract credentials from password managers, web browsers, or credential vaults to expand access.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries query system credential stores (e.g. Windows Vault, DPAPI) or target known browser database files containing saved credentials.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified extracted strings referencing credential storage, tokens, or passwords.
rules.hypothesis: the sample contains strings suggesting intent to query or interact with stored credentials
rules.explanation: Credential-related strings support a possible credential access hypothesis.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may query detailed system information such as operating system version, hardware architecture, computer name, and patch levels.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries call system APIs (such as GetVersionEx, GetSystemInfo, GetComputerName) to fingerprint the execution environment before executing conditional payloads.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified imported APIs dedicated to system information querying and environment fingerprinting.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may query system architecture, OS version, or environment metadata to fingerprint the host
rules.explanation: System information APIs support a possible host fingerprinting/discovery capability.

rules.label: POSSIBLE
rules.description: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or search in specific locations to find configuration files, sensitive documents, or target binaries.
rules.how_it_works: Adversaries iterate through filesystem paths using directory traversal APIs (FindFirstFile, FindNextFile) to locate target user data or system paths.
rules.why_igris_mapped: IGRIS identified imported filesystem enumeration APIs.
rules.hypothesis: the sample may enumerate local files and directories to discover target data or configuration files
rules.explanation: Filesystem enumeration APIs support a possible file and directory discovery capability.
